fact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing (1969) than to the construction of the Great Pyramid of Giza (around 2560 BC).
explanation: She died in 30 BC, roughly 2,500 years after the pyramid was built but only about 2,000 years before Apollo 11.

fact: Oxford University was already teaching students before the Aztec Empire was founded; teaching at Oxford began around 1096, while Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325.
explanation: Oxford predates one of the great pre-Columbian American empires by more than two centuries.

fact: Harvard University was founded in 1636, before Isaac Newton was born in 1643.
explanation: America's oldest university predates the era of classical physics.

fact: The last execution by guillotine in France took place on September 10, 1977, when Hamida Djandoubi was put to death in Marseille.
explanation: France abolished the death penalty in 1981, but the guillotine remained in use until that final execution.

fact: Woolly mammoths still roamed Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean as late as around 1650 BC, while the Great Pyramid of Giza had already stood for nearly 1,000 years.
explanation: A small isolated population survived long after mammoths went extinct on the mainland.

fact: The Ottoman Empire lasted from 1299 until 1922, more than 600 years, ending only after World War I.
explanation: It ended within the lifetime of people who lived to see the moon landing.

fact: The shortest war in recorded history was the Anglo-Zanzibar War on August 27, 1896, lasting roughly 38 minutes.
explanation: Britain bombarded the palace of a sultan it refused to recognize, ending the conflict almost as soon as it began.

fact: The Aztec, Mexica, and Inca empires existed at the same time as Henry VIII of England, who reigned from 1509 to 1547.
explanation: Cortes conquered Tenochtitlan in 1521 and Pizarro defeated the Inca in 1533, both during Henry VIII's reign.

fact: The Eiffel Tower was built as a temporary structure for the 1889 World's Fair in Paris and was originally intended to be dismantled after 20 years.
explanation: It was saved because it proved useful as a radio transmission tower.

fact: The Roman Emperor Caligula made his favorite horse, Incitatus, a priest and reportedly planned to make him a consul, according to Suetonius.
explanation: The story is used by ancient historians to illustrate Caligula's instability and contempt for the Senate.

fact: The fax machine was patented in 1843 by Alexander Bain, decades before the telephone (1876) or the lightbulb (1879).
explanation: Bain's device used a pendulum to transmit images over telegraph wires.

fact: Anne Frank and Martin Luther King Jr. were both born in 1929.
explanation: Their parallel birth year highlights how 20th-century history compressed dramatic global events into single lifetimes.

fact: The Hundred Years' War between England and France actually lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453.
explanation: It was a series of conflicts rather than a single continuous war.

fact: The Roman Colosseum could be flooded for staged naval battles called naumachiae, particularly in its earliest years under Emperor Titus around AD 80.
explanation: Romans dug a complex system of underground passages later, which made flooding more difficult.

fact: The Pony Express, a fast mail service across the American West, lasted only 18 months, from April 1860 to October 1861.
explanation: It was made obsolete by the completion of the transcontinental telegraph.

fact: The last veteran of the American Civil War, Albert Woolson, died in 1956.
explanation: He served as a drummer boy for the Union and lived to see the dawn of the atomic age.

fact: Construction on Cologne Cathedral began in 1248 and was not completed until 1880, a span of 632 years.
explanation: Work was halted for centuries before being resumed in the 19th century.

fact: The Spanish Inquisition was not formally abolished until 1834, more than three centuries after it was established in 1478.
explanation: It outlived the Spanish empire in much of the Americas.

fact: Queen Elizabeth II served as a mechanic and military truck driver in the Auxiliary Territorial Service during World War II.
explanation: She was the only female member of the British royal family ever to have entered the armed forces as a full-time active member.

fact: The Wright Brothers' first powered flight on December 17, 1903 lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet, less than the wingspan of a Boeing 747.
explanation: Their fourth and final flight that day lasted 59 seconds.

fact: Julius Caesar was never an emperor of Rome; the first Roman emperor was his great-nephew Augustus, who took power in 27 BC.
explanation: Caesar held the title of dictator perpetuo before his assassination in 44 BC.

fact: Saudi Arabia was founded as a unified kingdom in 1932, making it younger than many modern automobile companies.
explanation: Ford Motor Company, founded in 1903, predates the modern Saudi state by nearly three decades.

fact: The Titanic's wreck was not located until 1985, 73 years after it sank on April 15, 1912.
explanation: Robert Ballard's expedition used a deep-sea sled with cameras to find the wreck two and a half miles down.

fact: The word 'salary' comes from the Latin word for salt, 'sal,' because Roman soldiers were sometimes given salt allowances.
explanation: Salt was essential for food preservation in the ancient world and was a valuable commodity.

fact: The Great Fire of London in September 1666 destroyed about 13,200 houses and 87 churches, but officially killed only six people.
explanation: Historians believe the actual death toll, especially among the poor, was much higher but went unrecorded.

fact: Genghis Khan died in 1227, and his burial location remains unknown to this day.
explanation: His escort reportedly killed anyone they encountered to keep the site secret.

fact: The first crossword puzzle was published on December 21, 1913, in the New York World newspaper.
explanation: It was created by Arthur Wynne, a journalist from Liverpool, England.

fact: The Olympic Games were banned by Roman Emperor Theodosius I in AD 393 and not held again until 1896 in Athens.
explanation: The 1,500-year hiatus ended with Pierre de Coubertin's modern Olympic movement.

fact: The first message sent over the ARPANET, the predecessor of the internet, on October 29, 1969 was supposed to be 'LOGIN' but only 'LO' was transmitted before the system crashed.
explanation: The connection was between UCLA and Stanford Research Institute.

fact: Pope Gregory XIII introduced the Gregorian calendar in October 1582, and 10 days were skipped: October 4 was followed by October 15.
explanation: The change corrected the drift in the Julian calendar.

fact: Great Britain did not adopt the Gregorian calendar until 1752, skipping 11 days that September.
explanation: The transition led to widespread confusion but, contrary to legend, did not cause major riots.

fact: Russia did not adopt the Gregorian calendar until February 1918, after the Bolshevik Revolution.
explanation: The 'October Revolution' of 1917 actually occurred in November by the Gregorian calendar.

fact: The first traffic light was installed outside the Houses of Parliament in London on December 9, 1868, more than 25 years before the first practical automobile.
explanation: It exploded a month later and killed a police officer, leading to its removal.

fact: The world's oldest known recipe is for beer, recorded on a Sumerian clay tablet around 1800 BC, known as the Hymn to Ninkasi.
explanation: Ninkasi was the Sumerian goddess of beer.

fact: The Berlin Wall was constructed beginning on August 13, 1961, and stood for 28 years before falling on November 9, 1989.
explanation: It divided East and West Berlin throughout much of the Cold War.

fact: The Soviet Union officially dissolved on December 26, 1991, when the Supreme Soviet voted itself out of existence.
explanation: The hammer-and-sickle flag had been lowered from the Kremlin the day before.

fact: The Roman Empire technically lasted until 1453 in the form of the Byzantine Empire, when Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks.
explanation: The Eastern Roman Empire considered itself the direct continuation of Rome for nearly 1,000 years after the fall of the western half.

fact: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France, dedicated on October 28, 1886.
explanation: It was designed by Frederic Auguste Bartholdi with an internal iron framework by Gustave Eiffel.

fact: The Statue of Liberty's original color was a shiny copper, but it turned green over the course of about three decades due to oxidation.
explanation: The green patina actually protects the underlying copper from further corrosion.

fact: Pluto, discovered in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh, had not completed a full orbit around the Sun by the time it was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
explanation: Pluto takes about 248 Earth years to orbit the Sun once.

fact: The Eiffel Tower was the tallest man-made structure in the world from 1889 until 1930, when the Chrysler Building in New York surpassed it.
explanation: The Chrysler Building's reign as tallest ended within a year when the Empire State Building topped out in 1931.

fact: The longest reigning monarch in history was Louis XIV of France, who ruled for 72 years and 110 days, from 1643 to 1715.
explanation: Queen Elizabeth II of the United Kingdom came close, reigning 70 years and 214 days.

fact: The first photograph ever taken, View from the Window at Le Gras by Joseph Nicephore Niepce, was captured around 1826 or 1827 with an exposure time of about eight hours.
explanation: The image still exists at the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas at Austin.

fact: Constantinople was renamed Istanbul officially only in 1930, more than 470 years after the Ottoman conquest.
explanation: Although Turks had long called the city Istanbul, the formal name change came under Ataturk's modernization.

fact: The Library of Congress was burned by British forces during the War of 1812 in August 1814, prompting Thomas Jefferson to sell his personal library to rebuild it.
explanation: Jefferson's 6,487 books became the new foundation of the Library of Congress.

fact: Slavery was not abolished in Brazil until May 13, 1888, with the Lei Aurea, making it the last country in the Americas to abolish the practice.
explanation: Princess Isabel of Brazil signed the law, which freed roughly 700,000 slaves.

fact: The Magna Carta, signed in 1215, was annulled by Pope Innocent III just 10 weeks later.
explanation: It was reissued in modified form after King John's death in 1216 and gradually became a foundational document.

fact: Coca-Cola contained trace amounts of cocaine until about 1903, when the company switched to using spent coca leaves with the cocaine removed.
explanation: Coca leaves are still used today as a flavoring after the cocaine is extracted.

fact: Albert Einstein was offered the presidency of Israel in 1952 after the death of Chaim Weizmann, but he declined.
explanation: Einstein said he lacked the natural aptitude and experience to deal with people.

fact: The Tiananmen Square protests of 1989 ended on June 4, when the Chinese government deployed troops and tanks against the demonstrators.
explanation: The exact death toll remains officially unknown and disputed.

fact: The Suez Canal opened on November 17, 1869, after 10 years of construction.
explanation: It dramatically reduced the maritime route between Europe and Asia by removing the need to sail around Africa.

fact: The Panama Canal opened to traffic on August 15, 1914, the same month World War I began in Europe.
explanation: The opening was overshadowed by the outbreak of war.

fact: Operation Mincemeat in 1943 used a corpse with false documents to deceive Nazi Germany about the Allied invasion of Sicily.
explanation: The body, dressed as a British officer, was released off the coast of Spain and successfully fooled German intelligence.

fact: The Hindenburg disaster on May 6, 1937 killed 36 people, effectively ending the era of passenger airships.
explanation: The German airship was attempting to dock at Lakehurst, New Jersey, when it caught fire.

fact: The U.S. Civil War's bloodiest single day was the Battle of Antietam on September 17, 1862, with about 22,700 casualties.
explanation: The battle prompted Lincoln to issue the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation.

fact: The Mayflower brought the Pilgrims to Plymouth, Massachusetts in 1620, and roughly half of the original 102 passengers died that first winter.
explanation: Many remained on the ship through the harsh New England winter.

fact: The first transatlantic cable telegraph message was sent on August 16, 1858, from Queen Victoria to President James Buchanan.
explanation: The cable failed within weeks, and a permanent cable was not laid until 1866.

fact: Henry VIII of England had six wives in this order: divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived.
explanation: His marital history reshaped religious and political institutions in England.

fact: The Black Death pandemic killed an estimated 30 to 50 percent of Europe's population between 1347 and 1351.
explanation: The plague is now known to have been caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, carried by fleas on rats.

fact: The Treaty of Versailles, which formally ended World War I, was signed exactly five years after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand on June 28, 1919.
explanation: Franz Ferdinand was killed in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, sparking the war.

fact: The League of Nations, the precursor to the United Nations, was founded in 1920 but never included the United States as a member.
explanation: The U.S. Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles, blocking American participation.

fact: The Spanish flu pandemic of 1918-1920 killed an estimated 50 million people worldwide, more than World War I itself.
explanation: Despite its name, the flu likely did not originate in Spain; Spain reported on it because it was neutral and had no wartime censorship.

fact: Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, burying Pompeii and Herculaneum.
explanation: Recent evidence including charcoal graffiti suggests the eruption was in October rather than August, as long thought.

fact: The Tunguska event of June 30, 1908 flattened roughly 800 square miles of Siberian forest, likely caused by a meteor or comet airburst.
explanation: Despite the enormous scale of destruction, no impact crater was ever found.

fact: Alexander the Great died on June 10 or 11 of 323 BC at the age of 32 in Babylon.
explanation: Theories about his cause of death range from typhoid fever to poisoning, but the question remains unresolved.

fact: The Roman poet Ovid was exiled in AD 8 to a town called Tomis on the Black Sea, where he lived the rest of his life.
explanation: The exact reason for his exile remains unknown; Ovid himself blamed 'a poem and a mistake.'

fact: George Washington was inaugurated as the first U.S. president on April 30, 1789, in New York City, not Washington, D.C.
explanation: The U.S. capital moved to Philadelphia in 1790 and to Washington, D.C. in 1800.

fact: The Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 divided the newly discovered lands outside Europe between Spain and Portugal along a meridian west of the Cape Verde Islands.
explanation: It helps explain why Brazil speaks Portuguese while most of Latin America speaks Spanish.

fact: The first U.S. patent was granted on July 31, 1790, to Samuel Hopkins for a process of making potash.
explanation: President George Washington personally signed the patent.

fact: Joan of Arc was burned at the stake at Rouen, France, on May 30, 1431, at about age 19.
explanation: She was posthumously declared innocent in 1456 and canonized as a saint in 1920.

fact: The Vikings reached North America around AD 1000, nearly 500 years before Columbus, establishing a settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland.
explanation: The settlement was discovered and verified by archaeologists beginning in 1960.

fact: The Easter Rising in Dublin began on April 24, 1916, and helped catalyze the path to Irish independence in 1922.
explanation: British executions of the rebellion's leaders shifted Irish public opinion toward independence.

fact: Sliced bread was first sold commercially in Chillicothe, Missouri, on July 7, 1928, by Otto Frederick Rohwedder.
explanation: The phrase 'best thing since sliced bread' refers to this invention.

fact: The first official FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, with Uruguay defeating Argentina 4-2 in the final.
explanation: Only 13 nations competed in the tournament.

fact: The original 13 American colonies adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776, but most signed the parchment copy on August 2.
explanation: Only John Hancock and Charles Thomson are known to have signed it on July 4 itself.

fact: Thomas Jefferson and John Adams both died on July 4, 1826, exactly 50 years after the adoption of the Declaration of Independence.
explanation: Adams' last words reportedly included 'Thomas Jefferson survives,' though Jefferson had died hours earlier.

fact: James Monroe also died on July 4, in 1831, making him the third U.S. president to die on Independence Day.
explanation: No other president has died on July 4 since.

fact: Calvin Coolidge was the only U.S. president born on July 4, in 1872.
explanation: He inherited the presidency in 1923 after President Harding died suddenly.

fact: The U.S. Constitution was signed on September 17, 1787, by 39 of the 55 delegates to the Constitutional Convention.
explanation: Three delegates refused to sign, partly because it lacked a Bill of Rights.

fact: The Bill of Rights was ratified on December 15, 1791, four years after the Constitution.
explanation: It comprises the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution.

fact: The first nuclear weapon was tested at the Trinity site in New Mexico on July 16, 1945.
explanation: Lead scientist J. Robert Oppenheimer later recalled the line from the Bhagavad Gita: 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.'

fact: Hiroshima was struck by the first atomic bomb used in war on August 6, 1945, killing tens of thousands of people instantly.
explanation: Nagasaki was struck three days later, on August 9, leading to Japan's surrender on August 15.

fact: The United Nations was established on October 24, 1945, with 51 founding member states.
explanation: It replaced the League of Nations, which had failed to prevent World War II.

fact: The Berlin Airlift, from June 1948 to May 1949, delivered more than 2.3 million tons of supplies to West Berlin during a Soviet blockade.
explanation: At its peak, Allied planes were landing in West Berlin every few minutes.

fact: Nelson Mandela was imprisoned for 27 years, from 1962 to 1990, before becoming South Africa's first Black president in 1994.
explanation: He spent 18 of those years on Robben Island.

fact: The Vietnam War effectively ended on April 30, 1975, with the fall of Saigon to North Vietnamese forces.
explanation: It was the longest war the United States had fought up to that time.

fact: The Korean War (1950-1953) ended with an armistice but no peace treaty, meaning the two Koreas are still technically at war.
explanation: The Demilitarized Zone separating them is one of the most heavily fortified borders in the world.

fact: The Roman aqueducts brought water to Rome from as far as 50 miles away, and some still function today.
explanation: The Aqua Virgo, completed in 19 BC, still supplies water to Rome's Trevi Fountain.

fact: Julius Caesar was assassinated on March 15 (the Ides of March) in 44 BC, stabbed many times by a group of senators.
explanation: His death sparked civil wars that ended the Roman Republic.

fact: Constantine the Great moved the capital of the Roman Empire from Rome to Byzantium in AD 330, renaming the city Constantinople.
explanation: This shift effectively moved the empire's center of power eastward for the next 1,000 years.

fact: The first underground railway in the world, the Metropolitan Railway in London, opened on January 10, 1863.
explanation: It ran from Paddington to Farringdon and was initially steam-powered.

fact: The first FIFA Women's World Cup was held in China in 1991 and was won by the United States.
explanation: It was originally branded with M&M's as a sponsor.

fact: The Apollo 11 mission launched on July 16, 1969, and Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon on July 20.
explanation: Michael Collins remained in orbit aboard the Command Module Columbia.

fact: Only 12 people have walked on the Moon, all between 1969 and 1972 during the Apollo program.
explanation: Eugene Cernan was the last in December 1972 during Apollo 17.

fact: The Hubble Space Telescope, launched on April 24, 1990, was deployed with a flawed mirror that had to be corrected by astronauts in 1993.
explanation: The repair mission restored Hubble's sharp vision and enabled decades of discoveries.

fact: The first message sent via electric telegraph by Samuel Morse was 'What hath God wrought,' transmitted from Washington to Baltimore on May 24, 1844.
explanation: The phrase was chosen by Annie Ellsworth, the daughter of the U.S. patent commissioner.

fact: Alexander Graham Bell's first telephone call, on March 10, 1876, was to his assistant: 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.'
explanation: Watson was in an adjacent room in their Boston workshop.

fact: Thomas Edison did not invent the lightbulb but developed the first commercially practical incandescent bulb in 1879.
explanation: Earlier bulbs existed but burned out quickly; Edison's design lasted much longer.

fact: The Suez Crisis of 1956 saw Britain, France, and Israel invade Egypt after Egyptian President Nasser nationalized the canal.
explanation: U.S. and Soviet pressure forced the withdrawal of invading forces, marking the decline of Britain as a top-tier global power.

fact: The Cuban Missile Crisis lasted 13 days in October 1962 and is widely considered the closest the world came to nuclear war.
explanation: It ended when the Soviet Union agreed to withdraw missiles from Cuba in exchange for U.S. concessions, including the secret removal of missiles from Turkey.

fact: The Roman emperor Nero blamed the Great Fire of Rome in AD 64 on Christians, leading to the empire's first major persecution of them.
explanation: Historians remain divided on whether Nero himself was responsible for starting the fire.

fact: Pompeii was rediscovered in 1748, more than 1,600 years after it was buried by the eruption of Vesuvius.
explanation: Excavations have been ongoing ever since, revealing much about Roman daily life.

fact: Tutankhamun's tomb was discovered nearly intact in November 1922 by British archaeologist Howard Carter in the Valley of the Kings.
explanation: Tutankhamun was a relatively minor pharaoh, but the discovery made him the most famous of all.

fact: The Rosetta Stone was discovered in 1799 by French soldiers during Napoleon's campaign in Egypt.
explanation: It allowed scholars to finally decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs by comparing them with Greek and Demotic scripts.

fact: Jean-Francois Champollion decoded Egyptian hieroglyphs in 1822 using the Rosetta Stone.
explanation: He demonstrated that hieroglyphs combined phonetic and ideographic elements.

fact: The Roman Empire reached its greatest territorial extent under Emperor Trajan in AD 117.
explanation: It stretched from Britain to Mesopotamia.

fact: The Magna Carta was signed by King John at Runnymede on June 15, 1215, after his barons rebelled against him.
explanation: It established the principle that the king was subject to the law.

fact: Marco Polo traveled to Asia in the late 13th century and lived in or near Yuan-dynasty China for about 17 years, returning to Venice around 1295.
explanation: His book influenced European understanding of Asia for centuries.

fact: Christopher Columbus made four voyages to the Americas between 1492 and 1504, but never set foot on the North American mainland.
explanation: His voyages were to the Caribbean and the coasts of Central and South America.

fact: The first European to circumnavigate the globe was Juan Sebastian Elcano, not Ferdinand Magellan, who was killed in the Philippines in 1521.
explanation: Elcano completed the voyage in 1522 with only one ship and a handful of crewmen.

fact: The Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan had a population estimated in the hundreds of thousands in 1519, comparable to or larger than the biggest European cities at the time.
explanation: It was built on an island in Lake Texcoco and connected to the mainland by causeways.

fact: Machu Picchu was built around 1450 and abandoned only about 100 years later, near the time of the Spanish conquest of the Inca.
explanation: It was largely forgotten by the outside world until American historian Hiram Bingham brought it to international attention in 1911.

fact: The Inca Empire had no wheels for transportation, no draft animals, and no written language, yet built thousands of miles of roads and ran a complex bureaucracy.
explanation: They used a system of knotted strings called quipu to record information.

fact: Smallpox killed enormous portions of the indigenous population of the Americas after European contact.
explanation: The introduction of European diseases was a major factor in the conquest of the Americas.

fact: The Roman Empire's western half officially ended in AD 476 when the Germanic chieftain Odoacer deposed Emperor Romulus Augustulus.
explanation: Romulus Augustulus shared his name with both Rome's mythical founder and its first emperor.

fact: Charlemagne was crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day in AD 800.
explanation: His coronation revived the idea of a Roman empire in Western Europe.

fact: The Holy Roman Empire was, as Voltaire famously quipped in 1756, neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire.
explanation: It was a complex confederation of states centered in Germany that lasted from 800 to 1806.

fact: Napoleon Bonaparte was exiled twice: first to Elba in 1814 and then to Saint Helena in 1815 after his defeat at Waterloo.
explanation: He died on Saint Helena in 1821 at age 51.

fact: The French Revolution began on July 14, 1789, with the storming of the Bastille prison in Paris.
explanation: At the time, the Bastille held only seven prisoners.

fact: King Louis XVI of France was executed by guillotine on January 21, 1793, during the French Revolution.
explanation: His wife Marie Antoinette was executed nine months later, on October 16, 1793.

fact: The Reign of Terror during the French Revolution killed thousands of people by official execution between 1793 and 1794.
explanation: Many more died in prisons or during civil conflicts.

fact: The first manned hot air balloon flight took place in Paris on November 21, 1783, by Jean-Francois Pilatre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes.
explanation: The balloon was built by the Montgolfier brothers.

fact: Napoleon's army invaded Russia in 1812 with about 600,000 troops; only a small fraction returned.
explanation: Most died from starvation, disease, freezing temperatures, and Russian attacks.

fact: The Battle of Waterloo took place on June 18, 1815, ending Napoleon's rule and the Napoleonic Wars.
explanation: He was defeated by allied forces led by the Duke of Wellington and Field Marshal Blucher.

fact: The Congress of Vienna, from 1814 to 1815, redrew the map of Europe after the Napoleonic Wars.
explanation: Its diplomatic framework helped preserve relative peace among European great powers for nearly a century.

fact: The first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed on May 10, 1869, when a ceremonial golden spike was driven at Promontory Summit, Utah.
explanation: It connected the Central Pacific from the west with the Union Pacific from the east.

fact: Karl Benz patented his three-wheeled Motorwagen on January 29, 1886, in Germany, and it is widely considered the first true automobile.
explanation: His wife Bertha Benz made the first long-distance automobile journey in 1888.

fact: Henry Ford introduced the Model T on October 1, 1908.
explanation: He drastically cut production time using moving assembly-line techniques.

fact: The Crusades began in 1096 with the First Crusade and continued in various forms for nearly 200 years.
explanation: Pope Urban II called for the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont in 1095.

fact: The Knights Templar were arrested en masse on Friday, October 13, 1307, by order of King Philip IV of France.
explanation: Many were tortured and executed; the order was officially dissolved by the pope in 1312.

fact: The Gutenberg Bible, printed around 1455, was the first major book produced with movable type in Europe.
explanation: About 49 copies survive today, fully or partially.

fact: Johannes Gutenberg likely went bankrupt shortly after printing the Bible due to a lawsuit by his investor Johann Fust.
explanation: Fust took over the press, leaving Gutenberg in obscurity for years.

fact: The First Council of Nicaea in AD 325 produced the original Nicene Creed and helped standardize the date of Easter.
explanation: It was called by Roman Emperor Constantine to settle disputes within early Christianity.

fact: The First Crusade's siege of Jerusalem ended on July 15, 1099, with the city falling to European forces.
explanation: The conquest was followed by widespread massacres of the city's inhabitants.

fact: Saladin retook Jerusalem from the Crusaders on October 2, 1187, shortly after his decisive victory at the Battle of Hattin.
explanation: His relatively merciful treatment of the city's Christian inhabitants was widely noted by his contemporaries.

fact: Constantinople fell to Sultan Mehmed II's Ottoman forces on May 29, 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire.
explanation: The conquest is often cited as marking the end of the Middle Ages.

fact: The Spanish Armada was defeated in 1588 not primarily by the English navy but by a combination of English ships, storms, and poor planning.
explanation: Many surviving ships were wrecked off the Scottish and Irish coasts on the return voyage.

fact: The Gunpowder Plot of November 5, 1605, was a failed attempt by English Catholics to blow up Parliament and assassinate King James I.
explanation: Guy Fawkes was caught guarding the explosives beneath the House of Lords.

fact: The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) was one of the most destructive conflicts in European history.
explanation: It ended with the Peace of Westphalia, which established the principle of state sovereignty.

fact: The Salem witch trials of 1692-1693 resulted in 20 executions and the imprisonment of more than 150 people in colonial Massachusetts.
explanation: Massachusetts formally apologized for the trials in 1957.

fact: Peter the Great, Tsar of Russia from 1682 to 1725, imposed a tax on beards as part of his Westernization efforts.
explanation: Those who paid the tax received a token to carry as proof.

fact: St. Petersburg was founded by Peter the Great in 1703 on swampy land conquered from Sweden.
explanation: Tens of thousands of laborers died building the new Russian capital.

fact: Catherine the Great of Russia reigned from 1762 to 1796 after her husband Peter III was overthrown and killed.
explanation: She greatly expanded Russian territory and culture during her reign.

fact: The first census in the modern United States was conducted in 1790, counting about 3.9 million people.
explanation: The Constitution required a census every 10 years to apportion representation in Congress.

fact: The Louisiana Purchase of 1803 roughly doubled the size of the United States, costing about $15 million from France.
explanation: It included land that became all or part of 15 future states.

fact: Lewis and Clark led their expedition across the western United States from 1804 to 1806.
explanation: Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman, played a crucial role as guide and interpreter.

fact: The first ironclad warships fought each other at the Battle of Hampton Roads on March 8-9, 1862, during the American Civil War.
explanation: The USS Monitor and the CSS Virginia (formerly Merrimack) fought to a draw, ending the era of wooden warships.

fact: The American Civil War lasted from April 12, 1861, to April 9, 1865, with an estimated 620,000 to 750,000 military deaths.
explanation: It remains one of the deadliest conflicts in American history.

fact: Abraham Lincoln was shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theatre in Washington on April 14, 1865, just five days after Lee's surrender at Appomattox.
explanation: He died the following morning on April 15.

fact: The 13th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, ratified in December 1865, abolished slavery in the United States.
explanation: It was passed by Congress on January 31, 1865, less than three months before Lincoln's death.

fact: The first telephone directory was published in New Haven, Connecticut, in February 1878, listing only about 50 names.
explanation: It had no numbers; callers asked operators for connections by name.

fact: The Eiffel Tower's iron framework expands and contracts with temperature, growing about 6 inches taller in summer.
explanation: It was completed on March 31, 1889.

fact: The first modern Olympics were held in Athens in 1896, with athletes from 14 countries competing.
explanation: The marathon was added in honor of the legendary Greek runner Pheidippides.

fact: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York on March 25, 1911, killed 146 workers, most of them young immigrant women.
explanation: The tragedy led to major reforms in workplace safety laws.

fact: The RMS Titanic was the largest ship afloat when it sank on April 15, 1912, killing more than 1,500 people.
explanation: It carried fewer than half the lifeboats needed for everyone on board.

fact: Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie were assassinated in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip on June 28, 1914.
explanation: The assassination set off the chain of events that led to World War I.

fact: World War I ended at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month in 1918 with the signing of the Armistice.
explanation: Fighting actually continued in some places, and the formal peace treaty was signed at Versailles in 1919.

fact: The Bolshevik Revolution in Russia took place in October 1917 by the old Julian calendar, which corresponds to November 7 in the modern Gregorian calendar.
explanation: It overthrew the Provisional Government and brought Lenin to power.

fact: Tsar Nicholas II and his family were executed by Bolshevik forces on July 17, 1918, in Yekaterinburg, Russia.
explanation: Their remains were not officially identified until the 1990s.

fact: Mahatma Gandhi led the Salt March of 1930, walking about 240 miles to the sea to protest the British salt tax in India.
explanation: The march galvanized Indian opposition to British rule.

fact: India gained independence from Britain on August 15, 1947, with Pakistan partitioned off on August 14.
explanation: The partition led to one of the largest mass migrations in human history.

fact: The state of Israel was established on May 14, 1948.
explanation: It marked the end of the British Mandate of Palestine.

fact: The People's Republic of China was proclaimed by Mao Zedong on October 1, 1949, after Communist forces defeated the Nationalists in the civil war.
explanation: The Nationalists retreated to Taiwan, where they continued the Republic of China.

fact: The first kidney transplant between humans, performed in Boston on December 23, 1954, was between identical twins.
explanation: The surgery was performed by Joseph Murray, who later won a Nobel Prize for his work.

fact: Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a Montgomery, Alabama bus on December 1, 1955, sparking the Montgomery Bus Boycott.
explanation: Parks was a longtime civil rights activist, not the random tired seamstress of popular myth.

fact: The Soviet satellite Sputnik 1 was launched on October 4, 1957, becoming the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth.
explanation: It sparked the space race between the U.S. and U.S.S.R.

fact: Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space on April 12, 1961, aboard Vostok 1.
explanation: His flight lasted 108 minutes and circled Earth once.

fact: John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, Texas, on November 22, 1963.
explanation: Lyndon B. Johnson was sworn in as president aboard Air Force One about two hours later.

fact: Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech at the March on Washington on August 28, 1963.
explanation: The march drew an estimated 250,000 people to the National Mall.

fact: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated on April 4, 1968, at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, Tennessee.
explanation: He was in Memphis to support striking sanitation workers.

fact: President Richard Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974, becoming the only U.S. president to resign from office.
explanation: He left to avoid impeachment over the Watergate scandal.

fact: The Watergate break-in occurred on June 17, 1972, at the Democratic National Committee headquarters in Washington, D.C.
explanation: Five burglars were caught attempting to wiretap and steal documents.

fact: The Camp David Accords in September 1978 led to a peace treaty between Egypt and Israel, signed in March 1979.
explanation: Egyptian President Anwar Sadat was later assassinated in 1981, partly in retaliation for the treaty.

fact: The Iranian Revolution of 1979 overthrew the U.S.-backed Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi and established an Islamic Republic under Ayatollah Khomeini.
explanation: It led to the Iran hostage crisis, which lasted 444 days.

fact: The Chernobyl nuclear disaster occurred on April 26, 1986, in the Ukrainian SSR.
explanation: It is generally considered the worst nuclear accident in history.

fact: The Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, after the East German government announced that citizens could cross freely.
explanation: The announcement was a confused press conference, but the result was the opening of the border.

fact: The Maastricht Treaty, signed in 1992, established the European Union as we know it today.
explanation: It also paved the way for the euro currency, introduced in 1999.

fact: South Africa held its first multi-racial democratic elections in April 1994, leading to Nelson Mandela becoming president.
explanation: It marked the formal end of apartheid.

fact: The Rwandan genocide in 1994 killed an estimated 500,000 to one million Tutsi and moderate Hutu over about 100 days.
explanation: International intervention came too late to prevent the massacre.

fact: The Hong Kong handover from Britain to China took place on July 1, 1997, after 156 years of British rule.
explanation: The agreement included a 'one country, two systems' framework intended to last 50 years.

fact: The Hagia Sophia in Istanbul served as a Christian cathedral for nearly 900 years before becoming a mosque in 1453.
explanation: It was converted into a museum in 1935 and back into a mosque in 2020.

fact: The first FA Cup, the world's oldest football competition, was held in the 1871-72 season.
explanation: It was won by Wanderers, a now-defunct London amateur club.

fact: The Roman emperor Diocletian voluntarily abdicated the throne in AD 305, the first Roman emperor ever to do so.
explanation: He retired to grow cabbages at his palace in modern-day Split, Croatia.

fact: The Edict of Milan in AD 313 established religious tolerance for Christianity in the Roman Empire.
explanation: It was issued jointly by Emperors Constantine and Licinius.

fact: The Council of Trent, held in three sessions between 1545 and 1563, was a major Catholic response to the Protestant Reformation.
explanation: It defined many key Catholic doctrines that remain influential today.

fact: Martin Luther reportedly nailed his 95 Theses to the door of the Wittenberg Castle Church on October 31, 1517.
explanation: The act, whether literal or not, is traditionally seen as the beginning of the Protestant Reformation.

fact: The Treaty of Westphalia in 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War and effectively created the modern system of sovereign nation-states.
explanation: Historians still refer to the international system as 'Westphalian.'

fact: The British East India Company was founded in 1600 and at its height ruled large portions of the Indian subcontinent.
explanation: It was dissolved in 1874 after the British Crown took direct control in 1858.

fact: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late 1700s, with key inventions including the steam engine and the mechanized loom.
explanation: It fundamentally transformed economies, societies, and the global balance of power.

fact: The first commercial steamboat service was started by Robert Fulton on the Hudson River in 1807.
explanation: His ship, the Clermont, made the trip from New York City to Albany in 32 hours.

fact: The first cracker-style biscuits were originally a hardtack ship's biscuit eaten by sailors over months at sea.
explanation: Modern crackers evolved from these ancient long-lasting sailor's foods.

fact: The Roman emperor Hadrian had a wall built across northern Britain starting in AD 122 to mark and defend the empire's edge.
explanation: Long stretches of Hadrian's Wall still survive in northern England.

fact: The Greek mathematician Archimedes was killed during the Roman sack of Syracuse in 212 BC, reportedly while drawing geometric figures in the sand.
explanation: He was killed despite Roman general Marcellus's orders to spare him.

fact: The world's first university in the modern sense, the University of Bologna, was founded in 1088.
explanation: It pioneered many features of modern higher education.

fact: Coffee was first cultivated in Yemen around the 15th century and spread from there across the Islamic world.
explanation: Coffeehouses in 16th-century Istanbul became important hubs of social and intellectual life.

fact: Spain was officially still at war with Denmark from 1657 until 1981 due to a forgotten treaty that was never finalized.
explanation: The two nations had simply never bothered to formally end hostilities.

fact: The Roman dictator Sulla, who lived from 138 to 78 BC, voluntarily gave up his absolute power in 79 BC and retired to a country estate.
explanation: His unusual peaceful retirement was rare among ancient rulers.

fact: The city of Rome had over one million inhabitants at its imperial peak and did not return to that population until around the 20th century.
explanation: After Rome fell, its population dropped to perhaps 30,000 by the early Middle Ages.

fact: The Domesday Book, commissioned by William the Conqueror in 1086, is a remarkably detailed survey of land and livestock in England.
explanation: It is still occasionally referenced in English legal cases.

fact: The Black Death is believed to have entered Europe in 1347 through ships docking at the Sicilian port of Messina.
explanation: The fleet arrived from the Black Sea carrying infected sailors.

fact: The Battle of Hastings in October 1066 saw William the Conqueror defeat King Harold II of England.
explanation: Harold is said to have been killed by an arrow to the eye, an event depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry.

fact: The Bayeux Tapestry is actually an embroidery, not a tapestry, and depicts the events leading to the Norman Conquest of England in 1066.
explanation: It is roughly 230 feet long and was probably made in England in the 1070s.

fact: The largest empire in history by land area was the Mongol Empire, which at its height covered roughly 9 million square miles.
explanation: It reached its greatest extent in the late 13th century.

fact: The British Empire was the largest empire by population in history, at one point ruling about a quarter of the world's people.
explanation: At its height in the early 20th century, it covered about a quarter of the planet's land area as well.

fact: The first cookbook printed in English, 'The Forme of Cury,' was published around 1390 and was compiled by the master cooks of King Richard II.
explanation: It included recipes featuring exotic spices imported from Asia.

fact: The first chocolate bar was made in 1847 by Joseph Fry in Bristol, England.
explanation: Before that, chocolate had been consumed primarily as a beverage.

fact: Marie Curie remains the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911.
explanation: Her daughter Irene Joliot-Curie also won a Nobel Prize in Chemistry, in 1935.

fact: The Wright Brothers tossed a coin to decide who would try the first flight; Wilbur won but his attempt failed, so Orville flew first on December 17, 1903.
explanation: Wilbur made the longer flight later that day.

fact: Mount Rushmore was carved between 1927 and 1941, designed by sculptor Gutzon Borglum.
explanation: It was originally intended to depict each president from the waist up, but funding ran out.

fact: The Great Depression began with the U.S. stock market crash starting on Black Thursday, October 24, 1929.
explanation: The crash continued through Black Tuesday, October 29, when the market lost an enormous amount of value.

fact: Prohibition in the United States lasted from January 1920 to December 1933 under the 18th Amendment.
explanation: It was repealed by the 21st Amendment, the only constitutional amendment ever to repeal another.

fact: Sweden was officially neutral throughout both World Wars, though it traded with both sides in World War II.
explanation: Its neutrality was a longstanding policy that the country relaxed only in 2024 by joining NATO.

fact: The first dishwasher was patented in 1886 by Josephine Cochrane, a wealthy Illinois woman who was frustrated by her servants chipping her china.
explanation: Her company eventually became part of KitchenAid.

fact: The first artificial heart was implanted in a human, Barney Clark, on December 2, 1982, at the University of Utah.
explanation: Clark lived for 112 days with the Jarvik-7 heart.

fact: The first successful heart transplant on a human was performed by Dr. Christiaan Barnard in Cape Town, South Africa, on December 3, 1967.
explanation: The patient, Louis Washkansky, survived 18 days before dying of pneumonia.

fact: The Ford Motor Company introduced the 40-hour, 5-day workweek for its factory workers in 1926.
explanation: Ford believed that giving workers more leisure time would increase demand for cars.

fact: The first speeding ticket was issued in 1896 in England to Walter Arnold, who was caught going 8 mph in a 2 mph zone.
explanation: He was fined a shilling for his offense.

fact: The Boston Tea Party occurred on December 16, 1773, when colonists dumped 342 chests of British tea into Boston Harbor.
explanation: It was a protest against the Tea Act of 1773.

fact: Paul Revere's famous ride on April 18, 1775 was not a solo journey; William Dawes and Samuel Prescott also rode that night.
explanation: Revere was actually captured before reaching Concord; Prescott was the only one who completed the journey.

fact: The first battle of the American Revolution was fought at Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775.
explanation: It is the source of the famous 'shot heard round the world.'

fact: Benjamin Franklin was 70 years old when he signed the Declaration of Independence, making him the oldest signer.
explanation: Edward Rutledge of South Carolina was the youngest at age 26.

fact: The first U.S. Navy ship, the USS Constitution, was launched in 1797 and is still a commissioned warship today.
explanation: It is the oldest commissioned naval vessel afloat in the world.

fact: The Battle of New Orleans on January 8, 1815, was fought two weeks after the Treaty of Ghent had officially ended the War of 1812.
explanation: News of the peace had not yet reached the combatants.

fact: The Trail of Tears in the 1830s forced the relocation of Native American tribes from the southeastern United States to lands west of the Mississippi.
explanation: Thousands of Cherokee and other Native Americans died during the journey.

fact: The Alamo, in San Antonio, Texas, was the site of a 13-day siege ending on March 6, 1836, during the Texas Revolution.
explanation: Mexican forces under Santa Anna defeated about 200 Texan defenders.

fact: The California Gold Rush began with the discovery of gold at Sutter's Mill on January 24, 1848.
explanation: Within a few years, San Francisco's population exploded from a few hundred to tens of thousands.

fact: The Erie Canal opened in 1825, connecting the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean via the Hudson River.
explanation: It dramatically reduced shipping costs and helped New York become America's largest city.

fact: The first hot-air balloon human passengers were a sheep, a duck, and a rooster, sent up by the Montgolfier brothers in September 1783.
explanation: The three animals landed safely, paving the way for human flight two months later.

fact: The first photograph of a person was an accident; Louis Daguerre's 1838 image of Paris's Boulevard du Temple included a man getting his boots polished.
explanation: Other people moving on the street did not appear due to the long exposure time.

fact: The word 'bankrupt' comes from the Italian 'banca rotta,' meaning 'broken bench,' referring to the practice of breaking the table of an insolvent moneychanger.
explanation: It dates from medieval Italian banking practices.

fact: Florence Nightingale's nursing work in the Crimean War (1853-1856) helped establish modern professional nursing.
explanation: She also pioneered statistical visualizations like the polar area diagram.

fact: The phrase 'mind your Ps and Qs' likely originated in printing shops, where typesetters had to distinguish between mirror-image lowercase p and q letters.
explanation: It also has competing origin stories from bartending and dance instruction.

fact: The Brooklyn Bridge, opened in 1883, was at the time the longest suspension bridge in the world.
explanation: Its chief engineer, Washington Roebling, supervised much of its construction while bedridden with the bends.

fact: The Spanish-American War of 1898 lasted only about ten weeks and resulted in the United States gaining Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines.
explanation: Cuba was also freed from Spanish rule but became a U.S. protectorate.

fact: The phrase 'remember the Maine' refers to the USS Maine, which exploded in Havana Harbor on February 15, 1898, helping push the U.S. into war with Spain.
explanation: Modern investigations suggest the explosion was probably an accident, not Spanish sabotage.

fact: Theodore Roosevelt was the youngest person ever to assume the U.S. presidency, becoming president at age 42 in 1901 after the assassination of William McKinley.
explanation: John F. Kennedy was the youngest ever elected, at age 43.

fact: The Wright Brothers ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, before turning their attention to flight.
explanation: Their experience with light, strong, balanced bicycles informed their approach to aircraft design.

fact: The first synthesized plastic, Bakelite, was invented by Leo Baekeland in 1907.
explanation: It marked the beginning of the modern plastics industry.

fact: Roald Amundsen's expedition reached the South Pole on December 14, 1911, beating Robert Falcon Scott's British expedition by about a month.
explanation: Scott's team reached the pole but died on the return journey.

fact: Antarctica was the last continent to be discovered, with confirmed sightings beginning in 1820.
explanation: The first confirmed landing on the mainland is debated, but occurred in the 1820s or 1890s.

fact: Vatican City, the world's smallest independent state, was established on February 11, 1929, by the Lateran Treaty between the Holy See and Italy.
explanation: It covers about 49 hectares (roughly 121 acres).

fact: The Empire State Building, completed in 1931, was built in just 410 days during the Great Depression.
explanation: It remained the world's tallest building until 1970.

fact: The Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco opened to vehicle traffic on May 28, 1937.
explanation: It was the longest suspension bridge in the world at the time.

fact: Pearl Harbor was attacked by Imperial Japan on December 7, 1941, prompting the United States to enter World War II.
explanation: President Franklin D. Roosevelt called December 7 'a date which will live in infamy.'

fact: The D-Day Normandy landings on June 6, 1944, involved more than 156,000 Allied troops.
explanation: It was the largest seaborne invasion in history.

fact: The Battle of the Bulge, fought from December 1944 to January 1945, was the costliest single battle for the U.S. Army in World War II.
explanation: More than 19,000 American soldiers were killed.

fact: The Tehran Conference in November-December 1943 was the first meeting of the 'Big Three' Allied leaders: Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin.
explanation: It laid plans for the D-Day invasion and post-war boundaries.

fact: The Yalta Conference in February 1945 saw Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin shape the post-war world.
explanation: It included controversial decisions about Eastern Europe that would set the stage for the Cold War.

fact: V-E Day, marking victory in Europe in World War II, fell on May 8, 1945.
explanation: V-J Day, marking the formal surrender of Japan, occurred on September 2, 1945.

fact: The Marshall Plan, announced in 1947, provided about $13 billion in American aid to rebuild Western Europe after World War II.
explanation: It is considered one of the most successful foreign aid programs in history.

fact: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) was founded on April 4, 1949, with 12 founding members.
explanation: It was created as a collective defense alliance against Soviet expansion.

fact: The Warsaw Pact was the Soviet-led counterpart to NATO, established in 1955 in response to West Germany joining NATO.
explanation: It was formally dissolved in July 1991, shortly before the end of the Soviet Union.

fact: The Eisenhower Doctrine, announced in 1957, committed the U.S. to assisting Middle Eastern nations resisting communism.
explanation: It was triggered by the geopolitical fallout of the Suez Crisis.

fact: The Hungarian Revolution of 1956 was a popular uprising against Soviet-imposed communist rule.
explanation: Soviet forces crushed the revolt within weeks, but the events damaged Soviet legitimacy in Eastern Europe.

fact: The Prague Spring of 1968 was a brief liberalization in communist Czechoslovakia that was ended by a Warsaw Pact invasion in August.
explanation: It became a symbol of resistance to Soviet-style communism.

fact: The Cultural Revolution in China, launched by Mao Zedong in 1966, lasted until his death in 1976.
explanation: It caused massive social and economic upheaval and the persecution of many intellectuals.

fact: The Great Leap Forward in China (1958-1962) was an attempt at rapid industrialization that led to a devastating famine.
explanation: Estimates of the death toll vary widely but are generally in the tens of millions.

fact: The Six-Day War in June 1967 saw Israel defeat the combined forces of Egypt, Jordan, and Syria.
explanation: Israel gained control of the Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights.

fact: The Yom Kippur War began on October 6, 1973, when Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack on Israel.
explanation: It led to the OPEC oil embargo and a major global economic shock.

fact: The Cambodian genocide under the Khmer Rouge (1975-1979) killed an estimated 1.5 to 2 million people, about a quarter of the population.
explanation: Pol Pot's regime aimed to create an agrarian utopia by emptying the cities.

fact: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan began in December 1979 and lasted until February 1989.
explanation: It became known as the Soviet Union's 'Vietnam' and contributed to its eventual collapse.

fact: The Falklands War between the United Kingdom and Argentina lasted from April to June 1982.
explanation: Britain regained control of the Falkland Islands after Argentine forces had invaded.

fact: The Persian Gulf War to liberate Kuwait from Iraqi occupation in 1991 lasted six weeks, with the ground campaign taking only 100 hours.
explanation: The war was sparked by Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in August 1990.

fact: The Yugoslav Wars of the 1990s broke up the country of Yugoslavia into seven independent states.
explanation: They were the deadliest conflicts in Europe since World War II.

fact: The Bosnian War (1992-1995) included the Srebrenica massacre in July 1995, in which more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed.
explanation: It is the only event in Europe since WWII formally recognized as genocide by international courts.

fact: The Channel Tunnel between England and France opened on May 6, 1994, after six years of construction.
explanation: It is currently the longest underwater tunnel in the world by sub-sea length.

fact: The first website was launched on August 6, 1991, by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in Switzerland.
explanation: It explained how the World Wide Web worked.

fact: IBM unveiled its first personal computer, the IBM 5150, on August 12, 1981.
explanation: Its open architecture led to the dominance of IBM-compatible PCs.

fact: Apple Computer was founded on April 1, 1976, by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne.
explanation: Wayne sold his 10% stake for $800 within two weeks of founding.

fact: Microsoft was founded by Bill Gates and Paul Allen on April 4, 1975, in Albuquerque, New Mexico.
explanation: It moved to its current home in the Seattle area in 1979.

fact: The Macintosh computer was unveiled by Apple on January 24, 1984, with a famous Super Bowl commercial directed by Ridley Scott.
explanation: It popularized the graphical user interface and the mouse.

fact: The CD-ROM, capable of holding far more data than a floppy disk, was introduced commercially in the mid-1980s.
explanation: It became standard in personal computers by the mid-1990s.

fact: The first cell phone call was made by Motorola engineer Martin Cooper on April 3, 1973, in New York City.
explanation: He famously called a rival at Bell Labs to brag about the achievement.

fact: Walt Disney World in Florida opened on October 1, 1971, five years after Walt Disney's death.
explanation: It is many times larger than the original Disneyland in California.

fact: Disneyland in Anaheim, California, opened on July 17, 1955.
explanation: The opening was beset with problems and was later called 'Black Sunday' by Disney staff.

fact: The first McDonald's restaurant opened in 1940 in San Bernardino, California, by Richard and Maurice McDonald.
explanation: Ray Kroc began franchising it nationally in the 1950s and eventually bought the company.

fact: Coca-Cola was invented in 1886 by pharmacist John Pemberton in Atlanta, Georgia.
explanation: He died just two years later, before the product became widely successful.

fact: Pepsi was invented in 1893 by Caleb Bradham in New Bern, North Carolina.
explanation: He originally called it 'Brad's Drink' before renaming it Pepsi-Cola in 1898.

fact: The chocolate chip cookie was invented around 1938 by Ruth Wakefield at the Toll House Inn in Whitman, Massachusetts.
explanation: Her recipe became famous when it was printed on Nestle chocolate bars.

fact: The Slinky was invented in 1943 by Richard James, a naval engineer who knocked some springs off a shelf.
explanation: It was first sold at a Gimbels department store in Philadelphia in November 1945.

fact: The Frisbee evolved from pie tins thrown by Yale students from the Frisbie Pie Company.
explanation: Walter Frederick Morrison and Wham-O commercialized the plastic version in 1957.

fact: Velcro was invented in 1948 by Swiss engineer George de Mestral after he noticed burrs sticking to his dog's fur.
explanation: He patented the hook-and-loop fastener in 1955.

fact: Post-it Notes were invented in 1968 by 3M scientist Spencer Silver, who created a weak adhesive he didn't know what to do with.
explanation: Colleague Art Fry used the adhesive on bookmarks for his hymnal, leading to the product launch in 1980.

fact: The microwave oven was invented in 1945 by Percy Spencer after he noticed a chocolate bar melted in his pocket near a radar magnetron.
explanation: The first commercial microwave was sold by Raytheon shortly afterward.

fact: The Slinky toy has appeared in everything from a Buzz Aldrin sermon to Bart Simpson's hands to a famous TV jingle.
explanation: It was eventually inducted into the National Toy Hall of Fame.

fact: Crayola crayons were first produced in 1903 by Binney & Smith.
explanation: The name 'Crayola' was coined by company founder Edwin Binney's wife Alice from the French 'craie' meaning chalk.

fact: Lego was founded in Billund, Denmark, in 1932 by Ole Kirk Christiansen as a wooden toy company.
explanation: The famous plastic interlocking bricks debuted in 1958.

fact: The first Barbie doll was introduced by Mattel on March 9, 1959, at the American International Toy Fair in New York City.
explanation: She was modeled in part on a German doll called Bild Lilli.

fact: The yo-yo originated in ancient Greece and is one of the oldest known toys, with examples dating back over 2,500 years.
explanation: It became a modern craze in the 20th century thanks to Filipino entrepreneur Pedro Flores.

fact: Chess originated in northern India around the 6th century AD as a game called chaturanga.
explanation: It spread westward through Persia and the Islamic world to medieval Europe.

fact: The card game bridge evolved from whist in the 19th century.
explanation: Contract bridge, the modern form, was developed in the 1920s.

fact: Monopoly, the board game, evolved from 'The Landlord's Game' patented in 1904 by Elizabeth Magie.
explanation: Parker Brothers later commercialized it in 1935 without giving Magie much credit.

fact: The first modern crossword tournament was held in 1978 in Stamford, Connecticut.
explanation: It was founded by Will Shortz, later the famous crossword editor at the New York Times.

fact: Scrabble was invented in 1933 by Alfred Mosher Butts during the Great Depression.
explanation: It originally went by the names 'Lexiko' and 'Criss-Crosswords' before being rebranded.

fact: Atari released Pong, the first commercially successful video game, in 1972.
explanation: It helped launch the home video game industry.

fact: Nintendo was founded in 1889 in Kyoto, Japan, as a maker of hanafuda playing cards.
explanation: It branched into electronic games in the 1970s before becoming a global gaming powerhouse.

fact: The Sony Walkman was introduced in 1979, transforming the way people listened to music.
explanation: It made personal portable music a mainstream phenomenon.

fact: The compact disc was developed jointly by Philips and Sony, with the first commercial CDs released in 1982.
explanation: The format's storage capacity was reportedly set so that Beethoven's Ninth Symphony could fit on a single disc.

fact: The Boeing 747, often called the 'Jumbo Jet,' first entered commercial service in January 1970 with Pan Am.
explanation: It revolutionized long-distance air travel.

fact: The Concorde supersonic airliner began commercial flights in 1976 and was retired in 2003.
explanation: It could fly from New York to London in under 3.5 hours.

fact: The Hindenburg airship was filled with hydrogen rather than helium because the United States had restricted helium exports to Germany.
explanation: Hydrogen's flammability contributed to the disaster in 1937.

fact: The first jet airliner in regular service was the de Havilland Comet, which entered service in 1952.
explanation: A series of fatal accidents due to metal fatigue grounded it temporarily.

fact: The first nonstop solo transatlantic flight was made by Charles Lindbergh on May 20-21, 1927, in the Spirit of St. Louis.
explanation: He flew from Long Island to Paris, taking about 33.5 hours.

fact: Amelia Earhart became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean on May 20-21, 1932.
explanation: She vanished over the Pacific in 1937 while attempting to circumnavigate the globe.

fact: The first to fly nonstop across the Atlantic were British aviators John Alcock and Arthur Brown in June 1919, eight years before Lindbergh.
explanation: Their flight was from Newfoundland to Ireland.

fact: The Spirit of St. Louis is now displayed at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum.
explanation: Lindbergh donated the plane to the Smithsonian in 1928.

fact: The first powered submarine, the Nautilus, was built by Robert Fulton and successfully tested in 1800.
explanation: It used a hand-cranked propeller for underwater propulsion.

fact: The first nuclear-powered submarine, USS Nautilus, was launched in 1954.
explanation: It was named in homage to Robert Fulton's much earlier vessel.

fact: The Roman Republic was founded around 509 BC after the overthrow of the last king, Tarquinius Superbus.
explanation: It lasted until the rise of Augustus as Rome's first emperor in 27 BC.

fact: The Etruscans dominated central Italy before the rise of Rome and heavily influenced early Roman culture.
explanation: Many features of Roman religion, architecture, and politics had Etruscan roots.

fact: The Phoenicians invented one of the earliest alphabets around 1050 BC, which became the basis for the Greek and Latin alphabets.
explanation: Their script was carried across the Mediterranean by their trading networks.

fact: Carthage, founded by Phoenicians around 814 BC in modern Tunisia, was the great rival of Rome in the Punic Wars.
explanation: The Romans famously destroyed Carthage in 146 BC.

fact: Hannibal Barca crossed the Alps with his army, including elephants, in 218 BC to attack Rome in the Second Punic War.
explanation: Most of his elephants did not survive the crossing.

fact: The Roman politician Cato the Elder ended every speech with 'Carthago delenda est'—'Carthage must be destroyed.'
explanation: His persistent rhetoric helped lead to the Third Punic War.

fact: The Persian Empire under Cyrus the Great in the 6th century BC was the largest empire the world had yet seen.
explanation: Cyrus is also famous for releasing the Jews from Babylonian captivity.

fact: The Battle of Marathon in 490 BC saw Athens defeat a much larger Persian army.
explanation: It inspired the modern marathon footrace, named for the legendary runner Pheidippides.

fact: The Battle of Thermopylae in 480 BC saw a small Greek force, including 300 Spartans, hold off a vast Persian army for three days.
explanation: Though Greek forces ultimately lost, the battle has become iconic for its courageous last stand.

fact: The Greek philosopher Socrates was sentenced to death in 399 BC by drinking hemlock.
explanation: He was convicted on charges of impiety and corrupting the youth of Athens.

fact: Alexander the Great was a student of the philosopher Aristotle.
explanation: Aristotle was hired by Alexander's father Philip II of Macedon.

fact: The Library of Alexandria was founded by Ptolemy I or his son Ptolemy II in the 3rd century BC.
explanation: It aimed to collect the world's knowledge.

fact: Hypatia of Alexandria was one of the foremost philosophers and mathematicians of the late 4th and early 5th centuries.
explanation: She was killed by a Christian mob in Alexandria in AD 415, a turning point often cited in histories of intellectual freedom.

fact: The Mayan civilization developed independently in Mesoamerica, with major cities flourishing from roughly AD 250 to 900.
explanation: The Maya developed sophisticated writing, astronomy, and mathematics.

fact: The Maya used a base-20 number system and were among the first civilizations to develop the concept of zero.
explanation: Their calendar was extraordinarily precise.

fact: Teotihuacan, near modern Mexico City, was one of the largest cities in the world during the period from around AD 100 to 600.
explanation: Its name means 'place where the gods were born' in the much later Aztec Nahuatl language.

fact: The Olmecs, who flourished in southern Mexico from around 1200 to 400 BC, are often called the 'mother culture' of Mesoamerica.
explanation: They are famous for their colossal carved stone heads.

fact: The Indus Valley Civilization, flourishing around 2600-1900 BC, had advanced urban planning including drainage systems.
explanation: Its script has not yet been deciphered.

fact: Mesopotamia, in modern Iraq, is widely considered the cradle of civilization, with Sumerian cities arising around 3500 BC.
explanation: The Sumerians developed cuneiform, one of the earliest writing systems.

fact: The Code of Hammurabi, written around 1754 BC in ancient Babylon, is one of the earliest known law codes.
explanation: It established the principle of 'an eye for an eye.'

fact: Ancient Egypt's history spans about 3,000 years, from the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt around 3100 BC to the death of Cleopatra in 30 BC.
explanation: Even within Egypt, more time passed between the building of the Great Pyramid and Cleopatra than between Cleopatra and us.

fact: King Tutankhamun ruled Egypt for only about nine years, from roughly 1332 to 1323 BC.
explanation: He died at about age 19 of causes still debated by scholars.

fact: Ramesses II, also known as Ramesses the Great, ruled Egypt for 66 years in the 13th century BC.
explanation: He had more than 100 children and built monumental structures across Egypt.

fact: Hatshepsut was one of the most successful pharaohs of Egypt, ruling for about 21 years in the 15th century BC.
explanation: She often depicted herself as a man in royal art.

fact: The Pyramids of Giza were built during the Fourth Dynasty of Egypt, around 2600-2500 BC.
explanation: They were originally cased in smooth white limestone that has since been quarried away.

fact: Building the Great Pyramid of Giza is estimated to have taken about 20 years and tens of thousands of workers.
explanation: Most laborers were skilled paid workers, not slaves, contrary to popular myth.

fact: The Sphinx at Giza is thought to have been built during the reign of Pharaoh Khafre around 2500 BC.
explanation: Its nose was lost long before Napoleon's time, contrary to the myth that French soldiers shot it off.

fact: The Tower of Babel story in Genesis likely refers to a Babylonian ziggurat, possibly the Etemenanki dedicated to the god Marduk.
explanation: Ziggurats were stepped pyramid-temples common in Mesopotamia.

fact: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, may never have actually existed in Babylon.
explanation: Some scholars now believe ancient accounts may have been describing gardens in the Assyrian city of Nineveh instead.

fact: Of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, only the Great Pyramid of Giza still stands.
explanation: The others were destroyed by earthquakes, fires, or human action over the centuries.

fact: The Lighthouse of Alexandria, one of the Seven Wonders, stood for nearly 1,600 years before earthquakes destroyed it in the 14th century.
explanation: It guided ships into the harbor of Alexandria.

fact: The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, built around 350 BC, is the origin of the word 'mausoleum.'
explanation: It was built as a tomb for Mausolus, a satrap of the Persian Empire.

fact: The Colossus of Rhodes was a giant statue of the sun god Helios completed around 280 BC.
explanation: It stood for only about 54 years before being toppled by an earthquake.

fact: The Statue of Zeus at Olympia, made of ivory and gold by the sculptor Phidias around 435 BC, was 40 feet tall.
explanation: It was lost to history sometime in the 5th or 6th century AD.

fact: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus was famously burned down in 356 BC by Herostratus, who wanted to be remembered for the act.
explanation: His name was banned from being mentioned, but the attempt at suppression failed.

fact: The original Library of Alexandria suffered partial fires multiple times, including damage during Julius Caesar's siege of the city in 48 BC.
explanation: Its complete destruction was a gradual process spanning centuries.

fact: The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius's reflections, known as the Meditations, were never intended for publication.
explanation: They have since become one of the most enduring works of Stoic philosophy.

fact: The Antonine Plague (AD 165-180) is thought to have killed millions across the Roman Empire.
explanation: It may have been smallpox or measles brought back by soldiers from the East.

fact: The Plague of Justinian struck the Byzantine Empire from AD 541-549 and may have killed a significant share of the empire's population.
explanation: It is the first recorded pandemic of the Yersinia pestis bacterium.

fact: Justinian I's Corpus Juris Civilis, compiled in the 6th century, is the basis for civil law in much of the modern world.
explanation: It systematized Roman legal traditions in a form that has lasted to this day.

fact: The Hagia Sophia in Constantinople was completed in AD 537 under Emperor Justinian I.
explanation: It held the title of the world's largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years.

fact: The Arab conquests of the 7th and 8th centuries created an empire stretching from Spain to the Indus River.
explanation: This was one of the fastest territorial expansions in history.

fact: The Battle of Tours in AD 732 saw Frankish forces under Charles Martel halt the Muslim advance into Western Europe.
explanation: It is considered a turning point in European history.

fact: Baghdad was founded by Caliph Al-Mansur in AD 762 and became the cultural and intellectual center of the Islamic world.
explanation: The 'House of Wisdom' there preserved and expanded Greek, Persian, and Indian knowledge.

fact: The Mongol siege of Baghdad in 1258 destroyed the city and ended the Abbasid Caliphate.
explanation: It marked the end of the Islamic Golden Age.

fact: Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, founded the Yuan dynasty in China in 1271.
explanation: He was the emperor that Marco Polo claimed to have met.

fact: The Mongols failed twice to invade Japan, in 1274 and 1281, both attempts being thwarted by typhoons later called kamikaze, or 'divine winds.'
explanation: Japanese WWII suicide pilots took their name from these legendary storms.

fact: Japan's Edo period, from 1603 to 1868, saw the country largely closed off from foreign contact under the Tokugawa shogunate.
explanation: It ended with the Meiji Restoration in 1868 and Japan's rapid modernization.

fact: Commodore Matthew Perry of the U.S. Navy 'opened' Japan to trade with the West in 1853-1854 with a fleet of warships.
explanation: The encounter helped trigger Japan's modernization.

fact: The Boxer Rebellion in China in 1900 was an anti-foreign uprising suppressed by an international alliance of eight nations.
explanation: It further weakened the Qing dynasty, which fell in 1912.

fact: Sun Yat-sen led the revolution that overthrew the Qing dynasty in 1911-1912, ending more than 2,000 years of imperial rule in China.
explanation: He is considered the founding father of modern China by both the People's Republic and Taiwan.

fact: The Long March of Mao Zedong's communist forces in 1934-1935 covered about 6,000 miles in retreat from Nationalist forces.
explanation: Only a fraction of the marchers survived the journey.

fact: The Battle of Stalingrad, fought from August 1942 to February 1943, was one of the largest and bloodiest battles in history.
explanation: It marked a major turning point on the Eastern Front of World War II.

fact: The Battle of Midway in June 1942 turned the tide of the Pacific War in favor of the United States.
explanation: Japan lost four aircraft carriers in the battle.

fact: The Manhattan Project employed over 130,000 people at its height and cost about $2 billion in 1940s dollars.
explanation: It produced the world's first nuclear weapons in just a few years.

fact: The Nuremberg Trials, held from 1945 to 1946, prosecuted major Nazi war criminals after World War II.
explanation: They established important precedents in international law.

fact: Adolf Eichmann, a key architect of the Holocaust, was captured by Israeli agents in Argentina in 1960 and executed in Israel in 1962.
explanation: It is the only judicial execution ever carried out by Israel.

fact: The first international scientific collaboration in space took place in 1975 with the Apollo-Soyuz mission between the U.S. and U.S.S.R.
explanation: It marked a brief detente in the space race.

fact: The International Space Station was launched in 1998 and has been continuously inhabited since November 2000.
explanation: It is one of the most expensive engineering projects ever undertaken.

fact: Mongol Empire founder Genghis Khan was born around 1162 with the name Temujin.
explanation: He took the title Genghis Khan, meaning 'Universal Ruler,' in 1206.

fact: Timur, also known as Tamerlane, founded the Timurid Empire in the late 14th century and conquered vast territories from India to Anatolia.
explanation: He claimed descent from Genghis Khan and is one of the most feared conquerors in history.

fact: Ivan IV of Russia, known as Ivan the Terrible, was crowned the first Tsar of Russia in 1547.
explanation: He greatly expanded Russian territory but also created a brutal secret police, the Oprichnina.

fact: Vlad the Impaler, the Wallachian prince who inspired Bram Stoker's Dracula, ruled in the 15th century.
explanation: He earned his nickname from his preferred method of executing enemies.

fact: Elizabeth I of England reigned from 1558 to 1603 and never married, earning the nickname 'the Virgin Queen.'
explanation: The U.S. state of Virginia is named after her.

fact: William Shakespeare lived from 1564 to 1616 and wrote during the reign of both Elizabeth I and James I.
explanation: His birth and death dates are both traditionally observed on April 23.

fact: The original Globe Theatre, where many of Shakespeare's plays were first performed, burned down in 1613 during a performance of Henry VIII.
explanation: A cannon used in the play set fire to the thatched roof.

fact: Cervantes' 'Don Quixote,' published in 1605 and 1615, is often called the first modern novel.
explanation: It satirized the romances of chivalry that had been popular in medieval Europe.

fact: Galileo Galilei was tried by the Roman Catholic Inquisition in 1633 for supporting heliocentrism.
explanation: The Catholic Church formally acknowledged its error against him in 1992.

fact: Newton's 'Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica,' published in 1687, laid the foundations of classical mechanics.
explanation: It introduced his three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation.

fact: Sir Isaac Newton served as Master of the Royal Mint from 1700 until his death in 1727 and personally pursued counterfeiters.
explanation: He sent several counterfeiters to the gallows during his time at the Mint.

fact: The longest war in history is sometimes considered the conflict between the Netherlands and the Isles of Scilly (1651-1986), which produced no casualties.
explanation: It was formally ended in 1986 when a Dutch ambassador declared peace.

fact: Vincent van Gogh sold only one painting during his lifetime, 'The Red Vineyard,' in 1890.
explanation: After his death, his work became some of the most valuable in art history.

fact: Leonardo da Vinci's 'Mona Lisa' was stolen from the Louvre in 1911 by Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian who hid it for two years.
